title: He Gave This Landscape to a Museum in 1902. Nazi Germany Gave Him a Guided Tour in 1941.
standfirst: A Le Havre shipbuilder's son painted this Creuse riverbank as an unknown twenty-two-year-old and gave an early version to his hometown museum the following year. Four decades later, the same painter was vice-president of a Nazi collaboration group's arts section, one of six Frenchmen photographed boarding a train for a state-organised tour of the Reich.

sections.heading: Six Names on a Platform at the Gare de l'Est
sections.body: On 30 October 1941, a group of French painters and sculptors left Paris's [Gare de l'Est](https://www.galerie-roger-viollet.fr/en/photo-world-war-ii-french-artists-leaving-for-a-1012686-1094941406) for a fortnight's government-organised tour of Germany, travelling at the invitation of the sculptor Arno Breker and Otto Abetz, the Reich's ambassador to occupied France. A photograph taken on the platform that day, held by the Roger-Viollet archive, names six of the travellers: Charles Despiau, André Dunoyer de Segonzac, Maurice de Vlaminck, Kees van Dongen, André Derain — and Othon Friesz, sixty-two years old, forty years past the riverbank at Crozant, about to spend two weeks touring Munich, Vienna, Nuremberg, Dresden, Berlin and Düsseldorf as a guest of the power occupying his own country. [Other accounts put the full party](https://cactus.press/vlaminck/) at eight painters and five sculptors, including Roland Oudot, Raymond Legueult, Jean Janin, Paul Belmondo, Paul Landowski, Henri Bouchard and Louis-Aimé Lejeune. The trip, which ran until 16 November, [included a stop at Breker's own studio](https://y-a-s.over-blog.fr/2017/11/artistes-collabos.html) in Berlin.

sections.heading: The Excuse He Gave, and the One He Didn't Need
sections.body: Friesz justified the trip, when he was asked to, by pointing to promises that French cooperation might help free prisoners of war held in Germany, or to the simple need for artists to present a united front. That was a milder line than the one Vlaminck chose to put in print. [In June 1942, back in occupied Paris](https://www.lejournaldesarts.fr/le-voyage-en-allemagne-de-1941-la-photo-qui-derange-91179), Vlaminck used the magazine Comoedia to attack what he called cosmopolitan art, naming Picasso as the example of everything wrong with it — an argument no prisoner-release promise can explain away. Friesz's own role through the occupation was administrative rather than polemical: he sat as [vice-president of the plastic arts section](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Othon_Friesz) of the Groupe Collaboration, the Vichy-aligned cultural organisation that helped stage trips of exactly this kind.

sections.heading: The Committee's Answer Came in June 1946
sections.body: After the Liberation, the Comité national d'épuration for painters, draughtsmen, sculptors and engravers reviewed the wartime conduct of French artists, trade by trade. In June 1946 it ruled on Friesz: [a ban on exhibiting, selling or publishing](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Othon_Friesz) his work for one year, backdated to 1 September 1944, so that on paper it had already run its course by the time it was announced. [Vlaminck received an identical one-year prohibition](https://cactus.press/vlaminck/) from the same body. Both sentences were professional rather than criminal, nothing like the treatment reserved for collaborators convicted on graver charges, and Friesz was showing again well before the decade was out. He died in Paris on 10 January 1949, aged sixty-nine, a little over three years after the ban had technically expired.

sections.heading: Twenty-Two, Unknown, and Already Giving Paintings Away
sections.body: None of that was remotely foreseeable in 1901. Friesz was born in Le Havre to a family of shipbuilders and sea captains, not the kind of household that expected a painter. He met Raoul Dufy at the local lycée and [studied alongside him at the Le Havre School of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Othon_Friesz) before the two of them left for Paris, where Friesz also struck up a friendship with Georges Braque that outlasted the years their painting spent moving in the same direction. This particular riverbank belongs to a series Friesz painted on the Creuse at Crozant in 1901, when he was twenty-two. The following year he [gave one of those Crozant landscapes](https://www.muma-lehavre.fr/en/node/725), Vallée de la Creuse, to the museum in his home city — now the MuMa Le Havre — making him a donor to a public collection before he had much of a reputation to protect it with.

sections.heading: A Fauve on Paper, an Impressionist on the Riverbank
sections.body: The database behind this feature files the painting under Fauvism, and even Friesz's own biographers cannot settle exactly when that label started applying to him. [French-language sources place him at the 1905 Salon d'Automne](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Othon_Friesz), the exhibition that gave Fauvism its name, showing alongside Matisse, Marquet and Manguin. [English-language accounts instead date his membership to 1907](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Othon_Friesz), describing him joining a movement that already existed rather than helping found one. Either date leaves this canvas out of range: Friesz painted it at Crozant in 1901, years before he touched Fauvism by any account. [The museum that holds its companion piece traces its early debt](https://www.muma-lehavre.fr/en/node/725) instead to Armand Guillaumin and Camille Pissarro, Impressionists a generation older than Matisse — a style Friesz would leave for Fauvism and then, by 1908, leave again for what his biographers call a naturalism influenced by Cézanne.

sections.heading: Sixty-Nine Years, One Label
sections.body: Fauvism, generously read, occupied two or three years of a sixty-nine-year life that opened on a Le Havre shipbuilder's ledger and closed in a Paris flat, three years after a wartime suspension had already lapsed. The corpus needs one word for its movement column, and Fauvism is the nearest one that ever touched him, even though this canvas predates it by years and everything that came after it — the committee seat, the government tour, the year-long ban — has nothing to do with brushwork at all. A hundred and twenty-five years on, the riverbank at Crozant remains the one part of Friesz's record nobody has ever needed to argue about.
